lessons.title: Computing and virtual machines
lessons.outcome: Explain how a host, hypervisor, guest OS and application differ.
explanation: A physical server supplies processors, memory, network ports and storage access. A hypervisor divides these resources into virtual machines. Each VM has a guest operating system that runs applications.

A running VM is only one part of a working service. It may still need readable disks, a usable virtual network, identity, name resolution and a healthy application. Shared hosts create shared dependencies: several VMs can be affected by one host problem.

terms.meaning: The physical computer providing resources.
The layer that creates and runs virtual machines.
The operating system inside a VM.
Assigned processor capacity and memory; neither is storage space.

lessons.scenario: Three fictional application VMs stop together, but user laptops remain powered. Which shared dependency should you investigate?
options: The host and its resource/storage health
A single application identity permission
One laptop's local name-resolution cache
feedback: The shared host is a plausible common dependency. Check evidence before concluding it is the cause.
That check does not best fit the observations. The shared host is a plausible common dependency. Check evidence before concluding it is the cause.
That check does not best fit the observations. The shared host is a plausible common dependency. Check evidence before concluding it is the cause.

lessons.title: Ethernet switching and VLANs
lessons.outcome: Distinguish local Layer 2 forwarding from routing.
explanation: A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network. A VLAN separates a switch network into logical broadcast domains. An access connection typically serves one VLAN; a trunk can carry multiple VLANs.

A matching cable connector does not prove the logical network is correct. Physical link state, VLAN membership, allowed VLANs and virtual-switch attachment are different questions. A VLAN alone is not a complete security policy.

terms.meaning: A Layer 2 unit of network communication.
An address used in Ethernet forwarding.
A logical Layer 2 broadcast domain.
A link carrying traffic for multiple VLANs under an agreed tagging design.

lessons.scenario: A fictional VM link is up, but the VM was attached to a different training VLAN. What is the useful next check?
options: Compare the upstream route table before checking local attachment
Compare intended VLAN membership and virtual-switch attachment
Inspect the database service account before checking the local link
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. Compare intended and observed logical attachment before changing anything.
Compare intended and observed logical attachment before changing anything.
That check does not best fit the observations. Compare intended and observed logical attachment before changing anything.

lessons.title: IP routing and transport
lessons.outcome: Explain why a remote subnet needs a route and a return path.
explanation: Routers move packets between IP networks. Routing chooses a path toward a destination; switching provides local forwarding. One device may perform both roles, so identify the function rather than relying only on its label.

For a remote training service, investigate the local attachment, gateway, forward route, return route and policy. Reaching a router does not establish that the application, identity service or information exchange works.

terms.meaning: A Layer 3 unit carried across IP networks.
An IP network range used to identify local and remote destinations.
A next-hop router used to reach other networks.
A route for replies to reach the original sender.

lessons.scenario: A synthetic request reaches the remote training network, but replies cannot return. Which missing requirement best explains this?
options: Guest memory pressure on the application host
A client-side name-resolution cache
A usable return route
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. Request and reply paths both matter. Policy or service faults can also exist.
That check does not best fit the observations. Request and reply paths both matter. Policy or service faults can also exist.
Request and reply paths both matter. Policy or service faults can also exist.

lessons.title: DNS, identity and shared services
lessons.outcome: Separate name lookup, sign-in and permission checks.
explanation: DNS translates service names and helps clients discover services. Active Directory Domain Services uses DNS to locate domain controllers. A network path can be working while discovery or sign-in is failing.

Authentication asks who the user is; authorization asks what that identity may do. Time synchronization and certificates can also matter to services. Investigate each dependency using approved synthetic evidence rather than treating every failed sign-in as a transport outage.

terms.meaning: Name resolution and service discovery.
Information about identities and resources.
Checking an asserted identity.
Deciding which actions an identity may perform.

lessons.scenario: A synthetic user reaches the application, signs in successfully, but is denied a restricted task. Which area best fits the evidence?
options: Authorization for that task
The name-resolution service used before sign-in
The path MTU for the initial connection
feedback: Successful sign-in and a denied action point toward permission checks; inspect the actual denial.
That check does not best fit the observations. Successful sign-in and a denied action point toward permission checks; inspect the actual denial.
That check does not best fit the observations. Successful sign-in and a denied action point toward permission checks; inspect the actual denial.

lessons.title: Storage: files, blocks and persistence
lessons.outcome: Explain NAS, SAN and the difference between capacity and performance.
explanation: File storage presents files and folders, commonly using SMB or NFS. Block storage presents addressable blocks to a host, commonly through iSCSI or Fibre Channel. These are access models and protocols, not proof of compatibility with a particular Army stack.

Capacity describes how much data can be held. Latency describes response delay, while IOPS describes operations per second. A VM can be powered on yet unable to use an unavailable disk. A storage virtual machine in ONTAP is a storage-management construct, not necessarily a guest compute VM.

terms.meaning: File access over a network.
Block-storage access through a storage network.
A logical block-storage device exposed to a host.
Response delay and operations per second.

lessons.scenario: A training VM is on and reachable, but its application cannot read the attached data volume. What should you investigate?
options: The application's external DNS record
Storage availability, host access and the data path
The remote routing adjacency only
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. Storage is a separate dependency; inspect evidence without destructive changes.
Storage is a separate dependency; inspect evidence without destructive changes.
That check does not best fit the observations. Storage is a separate dependency; inspect evidence without destructive changes.

lessons.title: Firewalls and least-privilege policy
lessons.outcome: Explain why a route is different from permission to communicate.
explanation: A firewall evaluates traffic against security policy. PAN-OS policies can consider zones, addresses, applications, users and services. A routing decision and a security decision answer different questions.

For a fictional application flow, describe the source role, destination service, intended application and expected decision. Review synthetic policy and traffic evidence. Do not solve a denial by opening all traffic, and do not assume that a port number alone identifies every application.

terms.meaning: A logical grouping used in firewall policy.
A tracked communication exchange.
Conditions and actions governing allowed or denied traffic.
Allow only the access needed for the approved purpose.

lessons.scenario: A fictional route exists, but the simulated firewall records a denial for the needed application. What is the best next step?
options: Investigate the identity role before reviewing the recorded flow denial
Change the default route before comparing the denied flow
Review the intended flow and the matching policy with its owner
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. Reconcile the required flow with approved policy; no live device is changed here.
That check does not best fit the observations. Reconcile the required flow with approved policy; no live device is changed here.
Reconcile the required flow with approved policy; no live device is changed here.

lessons.title: Containers, orchestration and disconnected delivery
lessons.outcome: Distinguish an image, container, VM and orchestration platform.
explanation: A container packages an application and its dependencies while using the host operating-system kernel. A VM has its own guest OS. Containerization changes packaging and management; it does not remove network, storage or security requirements.

An orchestrator manages workloads across machines. Disconnected environments also need approved images, dependencies, registries and update processes available locally. An image starting successfully does not prove that data is durable or that the entire application works.

terms.meaning: A packaged template used to create a container.
A running isolated application process environment.
A platform coordinating workload deployment and lifecycle.
A service that stores and distributes container images.

lessons.scenario: A fictional disconnected lab cannot download a required image. Which planning gap should be addressed?
options: Approved local image and dependency availability
The cluster's external DNS record only
The running application's user permissions only
feedback: Stage approved artifacts and their dependencies using an authorized process.
That check does not best fit the observations. Stage approved artifacts and their dependencies using an authorized process.
That check does not best fit the observations. Stage approved artifacts and their dependencies using an authorized process.

lessons.title: Recovery, backups and availability
lessons.outcome: Define restoration evidence rather than assuming redundancy is backup.
explanation: Availability keeps a service usable. Recovery restores service after a failure. Redundant paths, replicated data and saved recovery copies address different failure cases; identify which failure the design is intended to survive. This lesson is an editorial exercise; full standard-text review remains pending.

A recovery exercise should use synthetic data and record what was restored, which user task works again, and how long recovery took. A copy that has never been restored is not sufficient evidence that the mission outcome can be recovered.

terms.meaning: The target time to restore a service.
The target limit on recoverable data loss, expressed as time.
A demonstration that recovery data can be used.
Components that may be affected by one shared failure.

lessons.scenario: Two training VMs use the same physical host and data volume. What has not been established?
options: That each VM has a separate guest operating system
Independence from host/storage failure and tested recovery
That the two VM applications can be restarted separately
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. A shared dependency can affect both VMs; test the intended recovery outcome.
A shared dependency can affect both VMs; test the intended recovery outcome.
That check does not best fit the observations. A shared dependency can affect both VMs; test the intended recovery outcome.

lessons.title: Security across the whole stack
lessons.outcome: Identify separate controls for identities, systems, data and operations.
explanation: Protect the management plane as well as user traffic. Separate administrator privileges, keep approved software baselines, protect secrets, inspect relevant logs and test recovery. A firewall cannot compensate for every identity, host or application weakness.

Teach least privilege through an observable task: a test user completes an approved action and is denied an unapproved one. Vendor features and secure-looking diagrams do not establish authorization to operate, a current hardening baseline or technical interoperability.

terms.meaning: Interfaces used to administer systems.
An approved set of versions and settings.
Records that help establish what happened.
Several complementary protections across dependencies.

lessons.scenario: A fictional user can reach the training app. What is stronger evidence of appropriate access control?
options: A successful reachability test from each client
A complete route table for the destination network
Authorized actions succeed and unauthorized actions are denied
feedback: That check does not best fit the observations. Test allowed and denied actions; document results and limitations.
That check does not best fit the observations. Test allowed and denied actions; document results and limitations.
Test allowed and denied actions; document results and limitations.

lessons.title: Cisco: Trace a client connectivity fault
lessons.outcome: Check the supplied addressing plan and locate the first failed network dependency.

terms.meaning: Logical LAN assigned to an endpoint port.
Router used to reach other networks.
Forwarding information for a destination prefix.

explanation: Compare the intended port assignment, client IP settings and gateway with known-good evidence. A link indicator proves physical link only.
After the path is verified, check the expected application transaction. Use the supplied address plan; no subnet calculation is required.
lessons.scenario: Which non-disruptive check best distinguishes a client or local port problem from a shared gateway problem?
options: Check the affected client and compare its port and supplied address settings to the approved lab baseline.
Reset the gateway for everyone.
Change all clients to a new address range.
feedback: This begins with the affected path and preserves the rest of the lab.
A working peer makes a shared gateway restart poorly supported.
A new address range introduces unrelated changes.

army_case.scope: The historical handbook establishes the role of WIN-T. Cisco switching is the classroom skill example. The workstation and port observations are invented.
army_case.task: At a fictional WIN-T classroom station, a staff workstation must send a training status report to an exercise reviewer.
evidence: The affected workstation sees physical link but cannot reach its assigned lab gateway.
A known-good workstation on another training port can reach the same gateway.
army_case.impact: The reporter cannot submit the update; the evidence does not establish a shared transport outage.
army_case.recovery: After the instructor resolves the fictional fault, the same workstation submits a fresh report and the reviewer confirms receipt and readability.

lessons.title: VMware vSphere: Trace guest network reachability
lessons.outcome: Separate a guest fault from a shared port group, virtual switch or host uplink dependency.

terms.meaning: A virtual network adapter presented to a guest.
A virtual networking policy grouping for connected workloads.
Host path from a virtual switch toward the physical network.

explanation: Start with scope: one VM, one port group, or multiple workloads on a host. Compare guest and host-side attachment before changing shared settings.
Verify reachability from the affected guest and complete the intended user task after an authorized repair.
lessons.scenario: Which comparison has the highest diagnostic value after the host move?
options: Restart vCenter immediately.
Compare the affected port group and uplink on the new host with the known-good path.
Rebuild both guests from backup.
feedback: Management availability alone does not identify the forwarding issue.
A shared dependency and a recent host change are both evidenced.
Rebuilding guests can leave the same failed network dependency in place.

army_case.scope: CECOM documents VMware-based TSI and a Hyper-V upgrade path for v5/v1. The fault and virtual network in this case are fictional.
army_case.task: A fictional TSI classroom host runs two guest services used to retrieve a practice staff report after a lab maintenance exercise.
evidence: Both affected guests were moved to another host and share one port group.
Guests on another port group still respond. Both affected guest consoles are available.
army_case.impact: Staff cannot open the report from affected guests even though the host and management console are up.
army_case.recovery: Repeat the report retrieval from an affected client and confirm that the same shared guest path works without disturbing the unaffected service.

lessons.title: Riverbed SteelHead: Separate pass-through from outage
lessons.outcome: Read the connection disposition and distinguish application reachability from optimization.

terms.meaning: Software platform used by SteelHead.
Connection reported as receiving optimization.
Connection forwarded without optimization.

explanation: Compare a fresh application transaction and its timing with the Current Connections report. Capture the disposition and reason for the same time window.
Pass-through alone does not establish an outage or justify changing a shared optimization policy.
lessons.scenario: What should you record first to tell an optimization issue from a service outage?
options: Declare the site offline.
Treat successful transfer as proof optimization worked.
Record the connection reason and compare transfer timing with a valid baseline.
feedback: The observed transfer completed.
Success and optimization are different measurements.
The reason and measured behavior provide two independent pieces of evidence.

army_case.scope: The historical WIN-T role supplies the training context. SteelHead is an illustrative WAN optimization product; the case makes no WIN-T appliance claim.
army_case.task: During a fictional WIN-T sustainment class, a staff user needs to deliver a training attachment before the rehearsal update.
evidence: The sample file transfer completes, but later than the classroom baseline.
The fictional optimization report marks the matching connection pass-through.
army_case.impact: Reports can arrive late even when delivery works. Confirm what actually failed before calling it an outage.
army_case.recovery: Have the sender repeat the same training transfer; verify receipt, measured transfer time and the report disposition as separate results.

lessons.title: Red Hat OpenShift: Diagnose a workload that never becomes ready
lessons.outcome: Use pod status, recent events and logs to tell a startup dependency failure from an application failure.

terms.meaning: Scheduling unit that runs one or more containers.
A recorded observation from a platform component.
Whether the workload is ready to receive service traffic.

explanation: Inspect pod state and recent events before assuming an application bug. Logs may not exist when a container never started.
For host troubleshooting, practice Linux service and storage fundamentals separately. RHCSA covers Linux administration; the OpenShift case is adjacent practice.
lessons.scenario: Which dependency should the learner check first?
options: Compare the storage claim status and expected class against the lab baseline.
Tune application logging.
Remove readiness checks so the workload looks healthy.
feedback: The event points to a startup dependency that can be checked directly.
Application logs cannot explain an event preventing startup without corroborating evidence.
Changing readiness does not bind storage or prove the application works.

army_case.scope: The Army source explains the C2 infrastructure transition. This case practices portable container troubleshooting using OpenShift as a classroom example. It does not identify a fielded C2NOW platform.
army_case.task: In a fictional C2NOW modernization classroom, a training team needs a containerized service to display a synthetic status report.
evidence: The workload remains pending. A lab event says a storage claim is unbound.
There is no application startup log because the container has not started.
army_case.impact: The team cannot publish a fresh training view. Repeated application restarts would not address the observed startup dependency.
army_case.recovery: After the instructor restores the configured lab dependency, confirm the workload is ready and the training user can open the expected fresh report.

lessons.title: Microsoft Windows Server: Separate DNS from application health
lessons.outcome: Compare the name lookup, expected endpoint and observed application response.

terms.meaning: Client or service that performs name resolution.
Published data that maps a name to information such as an address.
No applicable reply received within the observed interval.

explanation: Compare the failing name on the affected client with the expected resolver and a known-good peer. Distinguish DNS query errors from a service reached at the wrong address.
An application test by name remains necessary after the name result is correct. Where available, practice with Resolve-DnsName on a fictional lab host.
lessons.scenario: What is the best read-only check to isolate the name-resolution fault?
options: Reset the application service.
Test the name using the client’s assigned resolver and compare with a known-good peer.
Replace the server disk.
feedback: The evidence first points to a name-resolution difference.
This checks the failing dependency without a change.
No storage symptom is provided.

army_case.scope: CECOM documents Windows Server and Hyper-V in TSI modernization. This DNS case is transferable practice for a fictional hosted Mission Command service.
army_case.task: A Soldier supporting a fictional Mission Command classroom is asked to restore the instructor-provided service name for one staff workstation.
evidence: The workstation can reach the sample endpoint by address; the training hostname lookup times out.
A known-good workstation in the same exercise resolves the name.
army_case.impact: One staff user cannot open the shared training view by its normal name. Other users may still be working.
army_case.recovery: From the affected workstation, verify the expected answer and then open the application by name and retrieve the current training report.

lessons.title: Palo Alto PAN-OS: Explain a firewall traffic decision
lessons.outcome: Interpret a matched log record without confusing a rule action with successful application delivery.

terms.meaning: Policy entry used to decide how matching traffic is handled.
A policy grouping for traffic boundaries.
A logged indication of how a session ended, when available.

explanation: Match time, direction and service to the reported reproduction. Use the rule, action and session end reason to form a hypothesis.
An allow action by itself does not confirm service health. A denied synthetic session is evidence to review with the policy owner.
lessons.scenario: What evidence should you correlate before making a policy change?
options: Mark the user task successful.
Open all ports in the training policy.
Correlate the session end and return traffic with the server’s observed health.
feedback: The log action does not confirm delivery.
That change expands policy without evidence.
This distinguishes firewall policy from downstream service or return-path faults.

army_case.scope: The Army source supplies modernization context. PAN-OS is the commercial log-reading example. No C2NOW security product or policy baseline is inferred.
army_case.task: An authorized staff user in a fictional C2NOW support workshop must read a training status display across a classroom service boundary.
evidence: A sample log for the same transaction and time records an allow action.
The session times out and the user does not receive the training display.
army_case.impact: Policy allowed the attempt, but the staff task still failed. The issue belongs in the handoff until the application result is verified.
army_case.recovery: Have the affected user open the training display. Confirm the expected result and that unrelated denied access remains denied.

lessons.title: Palantir Foundry: Trace a stale dashboard to the pipeline
lessons.outcome: Use build status, timestamps and lineage to locate the first stale or failed input.

terms.meaning: A recorded execution of pipeline work.
Relationships tracing a dataset to its inputs and downstream uses.
Age of the data relative to expected updates.

explanation: A dashboard can render normally while presenting old results. Compare its data timestamp to the expected refresh time.
Use the affected build details and upstream lineage to identify the first stale input or failed change. Verify the resulting dataset timestamp and dashboard after recovery.
lessons.scenario: Which action starts the investigation of the stale training report?
options: Trace lineage to the first stale or failed input and inspect the associated build.
Reset every dashboard user’s permissions.
Treat the dashboard as current because it opens.
feedback: This connects the user symptom to the earliest evidenced dependency.
A permission reset does not address the observed refresh failure.
Rendering and freshness are separate.

army_case.scope: C2NOW is the synthetic data-support setting. The Army Vantage reference identifies Foundry for Vantage only. This lesson does not identify a C2NOW platform or model a Maven workflow.
army_case.task: A fictional C2NOW data-support class asks a staff reader to distinguish a current exercise report from a stale one.
evidence: The classroom dashboard opens and the user is authorized. Its display contains yesterday’s dummy data.
The sample build history reports that a scheduled upstream input failed.
army_case.impact: Readers can open the view but may brief the wrong exercise status if they trust the old data.
army_case.recovery: Verify a successful training build and a current timestamp, then have the staff reader compare the updated display with the expected synthetic input.

lessons.title: Dell PowerEdge: Correlate hardware events with host symptoms
lessons.outcome: Use hardware management observations to separate a component alarm from a guest OS symptom.

terms.meaning: Dell management controller for a PowerEdge server.
A chronological record of supported hardware and management events.
A warning state that warrants evidence gathering; it does not identify every affected application.

explanation: Check the relevant hardware health view and timestamps. Compare reports from the host and application before replacing components.
Collect only allowed diagnostics. Preserve logs and use authorized hardware support for corrective work.
lessons.scenario: What should you collect first to test whether the host alert explains the guest symptoms?
options: Clear the hardware history.
Correlate the storage alert and Lifecycle Log timestamps with guest and host symptoms.
Reinstall the DNS server first.
feedback: Clearing the history destroys useful evidence.
Independent timestamps help determine whether a shared storage problem explains the reports.
No name resolution symptom is reported.

army_case.scope: CECOM documents compute and storage as TSI dependencies. Dell management logs are a classroom example, with no claim about installed TSI server hardware.
army_case.task: A fictional Mission Command hosting team must determine why several training guests cannot save a staff report promptly.
evidence: Guest reports show slow writes within the same window.
A sample host management log records a new storage health alert.
army_case.impact: A shared host issue could delay several staff users; a single-application explanation is premature.
army_case.recovery: After authorized support resolves the fictional fault, repeat the same report save and read-back from affected guests and compare the result with the baseline.

lessons.title: NetApp ONTAP: Distinguish an NFS access denial from loss of transport
lessons.outcome: Compare client scope, applicable export policy and file permissions with a known-good client.

terms.meaning: Storage virtual machine that provides storage services.
Rules governing client access to an NFS export.
Storage object to which access policy may apply.

explanation: Compare whether the storage endpoint is reachable and whether it rejects the requested access. A permission denial can point to the export policy, protocol, authentication or filesystem permissions.
Verify the relevant client and export before any change. Retest only the intended access and confirm a client outside scope remains denied.
lessons.scenario: What evidence best separates an access problem from a shared transport outage?
options: Restart all storage controllers.
Grant all clients broad access.
Compare the affected client identity and protocol with the applicable policy and file permissions.
feedback: A responding authorized peer does not support a controller-wide outage.
Broadening access bypasses the diagnostic question.
This follows the denial and preserves the intended permission boundary.

army_case.scope: CECOM documents storage as a TSI dependency. ONTAP is an illustrative classroom storage product, with no claim about the installed TSI array.
army_case.task: A fictional Mission Command classroom user needs to read a shared training artifact from a hosted service.
evidence: The affected training client receives an NFS permission denial.
A known-good client can read the same sample export.
army_case.impact: Access for one training client is blocked. The evidence does not support a storage outage affecting everyone.
army_case.recovery: Verify the affected authorized client can read the required training file and confirm that an out-of-scope test client still cannot read it.

lessons.title: PacStar IQ-Core: Separate management visibility from user service
lessons.outcome: Corroborate a management status with a second observation and an authorized fictional user test.

terms.meaning: Summary of observations available to management software.
Periodic retrieval of status by a management system.
Observable action the exercise participant must complete.

explanation: A management dashboard and a user application answer different questions. Check when the dashboard last saw the training device, then compare a separate user task.
Report the observations and uncertainty to the authorized support role. This lesson uses invented outputs and supplies no deployment instructions.
lessons.scenario: What conclusion is supported by these two observations?
options: The observations disagree; record their timing and check the management observation path.
The user service is definitely unavailable.
Replace the device immediately.
feedback: Scope the management symptom and confirm independent evidence before changing equipment.
The observed user transaction succeeded.
The discrepancy does not justify replacement.

army_case.scope: The historical handbook describes WIN-T. IQ-Core is the commercial management example; the lesson does not infer it is present in the named WIN-T system.
army_case.task: During a fictional WIN-T support class, a Soldier must reconcile a management observation with a staff user’s training report exchange.
evidence: The exercise management view shows a device as unreachable.
The fictional staff user succeeds in sending a current report and obtains an acknowledgement.
army_case.impact: Management visibility is degraded in the exercise, while the demonstrated user function still works.
army_case.recovery: Confirm a fresh management observation and repeat the same staff transaction. Report any remaining discrepancy to the exercise support lead.

lessons.title: General Dynamics TACLANE: Recognize a status and support boundary
lessons.outcome: Record a fictional service symptom and distinguish platform identity from proof of service.

terms.meaning: Related models that require release-specific approved instructions.
An observation that may cover only one component.
A structured report to the authorized owner.

explanation: Public material identifies equipment families and vendor training. It does not establish which settings, access or procedures apply to a unit.
In this fictional case, report the visible status, time, affected user task and observations to the authorized owner. Leave approved equipment checks to qualified personnel.
lessons.scenario: What belongs in the handoff to the authorized support role?
options: A statement that all service is restored.
The discrepancy, time and affected user task, with a request for authorized review.
A proposal to bypass the protected boundary.
feedback: A device indication does not verify the end user task.
An evidence-based report preserves the boundary and makes the symptom actionable.
A safeguard is not an acceptable workaround.

army_case.scope: The historical WIN-T role frames the fictional handoff. The General Dynamics source identifies a product family, not an installed device or operating procedure.
army_case.task: In a fictional WIN-T support class, a staff user cannot retrieve a dummy report and asks for an evidence-based equipment handoff.
evidence: An instructor status card for the classroom device says healthy.
The expected staff transaction fails in the exercise at the same time.
army_case.impact: The receiving user is still blocked. An equipment indication alone does not verify service.
army_case.recovery: Have authorized exercise staff resolve the simulated issue. The affected user repeats the report retrieval and confirms that the result is readable.
